parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or material property damage to the regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a written incident report within 10 calendar days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a potential safety risk, and promptly provide updates as facts are confirmed.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or material property damage to the regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a written incident report within 10 calendar days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a potential safety risk, and promptly provide updates as facts are confirmed.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or material property damage to the regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a written incident report within 10 calendar days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a potential safety risk, and promptly provide updates as facts are confirmed. Reports must include the unit and model identifiers, incident circumstances, and known harm. Suspected incidents must be reported; reporting does not depend on a completed investigation.

parameters.quote: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Before purchase, customers must receive that model’s latest test protocol, sample size, and failure rate; these results may be provided to prospective customers for that model but must not be published for general public access. A failure rate above 5% requires prompt notice to the regulator and affected customers, a corrective-action plan, and retesting within six months. Regulators may impose proportionate restrictions, including sales restrictions, where evidence shows adequate safety cannot be demonstrated; exceeding 5% alone does not automatically prohibit sale.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Before purchase, customers must receive that model’s latest test protocol, sample size, and failure rate; these results may be provided to prospective customers for that model but must not be published for general public access. A failure rate above 5% requires prompt notice to the regulator and affected customers, a corrective-action plan, and retesting within six months. Regulators may impose proportionate restrictions, including sales restrictions, where evidence shows adequate safety cannot be demonstrated; exceeding 5% alone does not automatically prohibit sale.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers must submit per-model protocols, sample sizes, and results to the regulator before sale and after any material design change. Before purchase, customers must receive that model’s latest test protocol, sample size, and failure rate; these results may be provided to prospective customers for that model but must not be published for general public access. Retesting is required at least every two years and after a material design change. A failure rate above 5% requires prompt notice to the regulator and affected customers, a corrective-action plan, and retesting within six months. Regulators may impose proportionate restrictions, including sales restrictions, where evidence shows adequate safety cannot be demonstrated; exceeding 5% alone does not automatically prohibit sale.

parameters.quote: New units placed on the market after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer instructions. Existing installed units that can be retrofitted must be upgraded within six years of adoption. Manufacturers must notify owners of units that cannot be upgraded and provide appropriate alternative emergency guidance.

parameters.quote: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption. The suppression system must be suitable for the battery chemistry and foreseeable residential installation conditions, and must be tested as part of the model’s safety evaluation.

S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption. The suppression system must be suitable for the battery chemistry and foreseeable residential installation conditions, and must be tested as part of the model’s safety evaluation. Manufacturers must provide customers with instructions on system operation, inspection, and limitations.

parameters.quote: A mandatory recall is triggered when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, using model-specific incident and installed-unit data verified by the regulator. The manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers and implement the regulator-approved recall, which may use an appropriate corrective remedy; the threshold itself does not prescribe a particular remedy or automatically require a sales ban.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Halcyon’s flagship model has a 3.9% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test
ground_truth_claims.message_text: For evidence-based thresholds, Halcyon’s flagship model has a 3.9% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test, while its thermal incident rate last year was 9.9 per 100,000 installed units. Halcyon’s company-wide rate was 8.1 per 100,000. These figures underscore the need for customer access to model-specific test results and a clear, enforceable response when incident rates exceed the proposed trigger.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Northwind’s Hearth 10 had a 6.2% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test
ground_truth_claims.message_text: For comparison, Northwind’s Hearth 10 had a 6.2% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test and a model-specific thermal incident rate of 6.4 per 100,000 installed units last year. Northwind’s company-wide rate was 8.6 per 100,000. The Hearth 10’s incident rate is below the proposed model-specific 8-per-100,000 recall trigger; the test result supports keeping the 5% exceedance response proportionate, with corrective action and regulator oversight rather than an automatic sales ban.

judge_section_notes: The final rules are a compromise: S1 is strict on incident reporting; S2 adopts a 55°C/5% testing regime but does not automatically ban models exceeding 5%, instead requiring corrective action and allowing sales; S3 and S4 accept Halcyon's red lines (6-year retrofit, 36-month suppression) while S5 sets an 8/100k recall trigger with flexible remedies.
